Adult female Asian common toads attain a maximum snout-vent length of 8.5 centimeters [Li = 8.5 centimeters], a size that makes them one of the larger bufonids in their range. Males are slightly smaller, reaching an ultimate SVL of 8.3 centimeters [Li = 8.3 centimeters], with most individuals falling between 6.5 and 8.5 centimeters (6.5-8.5 centimeters) [Li = 6.5-8.5 centimeters] when fully grown. This modest sexual size dimorphism is typical of many Bufonidae, where females often grow larger to accommodate increased clutch volumes. Field surveys across Southeast Asia have consistently documented these upper size limits, with the largest specimens usually recorded from lowland populations where growing seasons are extended. The species exhibits a steady growth trajectory after metamorphosis, with age rather than environmental quality appearing to be the primary determinant of final body size in most populations studied.

Females undergo metamorphosis at a snout-vent length of 7 centimeters , a developmental milestone that marks the transition from an aquatic tadpole to a terrestrial juvenile. This size at metamorphosis is relatively large compared to many other Asian bufonids, suggesting that the tadpole stage is characterized by prolonged feeding and growth before the energetic demands of body plan reorganization begin. The metamorphic climax involves tail resorption and limb bud development, culminating in the emergence of a fully formed froglet prepared for a terrestrial existence. Such a tiny initial mass imposes substantial predation risk during the early juvenile phase, and the species compensates through high fecundity rather than through extended parental care or large offspring size.

This brief endotrophic phase is critical for allowing the tadpoles to disperse from the egg mass before beginning active foraging.

The reproductive output of the Asian common toad is among the highest recorded for any bufonid of its body size.
